item.title: When Suffering Is Confused for Strength
item.description:
Resilience

When Suffering Is Confused for Strength

How unnecessary pain becomes justified as resilience.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Needless suffering rarely leads to personal growth.
  • Resilience comes from freeing ourselves of unnecessary harm, not from re-experiencing it.
  • Perseverance can help us survive pain, but resilience can help us evolve beyond it.
Source: Muhammed Diler / Pexels

We’ve all heard the expression, “If you’re going through hell, keep going.” On the one hand, this phrase brilliantly encourages us to evolve through discomfort; to keep pushing through so we can come out stronger on the other side. From this perspective, we cannot grow if we don’t push ourselves out of our comfort zones and feel uncomfortable at times, mentally or physically.

On the other hand, this phrase can become an excuse to stay in a situation when conditions are poor. While we know pain equals gain at the gym, that is not always true in relationships, careers, friendships, finances, or other life circumstances. Discomfort doesn't always lead to evolution. Sometimes it's just needless suffering: pain that will not likely enlighten us just from the continued experience of it. Walking away from things, people, and places that could harm you or have harmed you doesn't make you a coward; it makes you the bravest version of yourself yet.

The Sunk Cost Fallacy

Letting go is not giving up. While these two experiences may have the same outcome, be it releasing a relationship, career, material possession, or otherwise, they have entirely different intentions.

Imagine still driving a broken-down car; the parts are rusted, the engine barely starts, the brakes are shot. You’ve put a lot of money and time into this vehicle, and while letting it go may even feel emotional, no one would judge you for it. In fact, you’ll be safer and go further in a different model. Giving up, in contrast, might look like trading in the car after you spill coffee on your seat.

Source: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels

When “going through hell” means ignoring safety risks and crossing your fingers, it might hurt you, or someone else. Likewise, choosing to stay in unhealthy life circumstances, which can range from irritating to life-threatening, will not help you evolve.

Suffering in what's familiar but unhealthy and calling it perseverance is an earnest but misguided perspective. One of the most difficult truths, here, is that all the time, money, and love we put into something or someone does not justify us holding on to it. The sunk cost fallacy does not deserve to run your life.

Letting Go of Justification

The strength you muster in your life will not come from the intensity of pain, but from your willpower to liberate yourself from it. Consider a time when you had no choice but to stay on your path, when circumstances were beyond your control. Here, resilience meant adapting to adversity and learning how to live in “hell.” Under these circumstances, you may have taken on a common adaptation to adversity, such as dissociation, people-pleasing, denial, self-blame, or toxic positivity.

Whether you’ve been used to denying the harsh realities of your life or blaming yourself for them, those adaptations can get in the way in situations where we do have a say. It is extremely important to acknowledge how adapting to adversity this way helped you at some point; maybe it even saved your life. Equally important is learning to trust that you, as an autonomous adult, have the power to save yourself now.

Releasing false justifications that once protected you from these harsh realities might be the kindest thing you ever do for yourself. This may feel uncomfortable, but it’s the sort of pain that leads to liberation, not stagnation.

Source: Dishant Babariya / Pexels

Growth by Liberation

Though hardship can foster perseverance, you don't deserve to live your whole life in survival mode. When we can change course, true resilience looks like accepting the reality of the painful situation we’re in so we can confidently step out of it.

Once we genuinely trust that we’re safe to do so, and that staying stuck is far scarier than changing course, resilience grows stronger with each step we take off the path that led us here. Then, we just might discover that bravely choosing a different path out of “hell” is the true roadmap to growth.

item.title: In Life, as in the Navy, He Knew How to Change Course
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

In Life, as in the Navy, He Knew How to Change Course

Personal Perspective: A lesson in making the most of our circumstances.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Being grateful for the lessons in challenging circustances can open us up to new experiences.
  • Embracing a difficult situation improves our perspective and possibly even the situation.
  • A positive attitude attracts positive energy, which tends to be contagious.

The following is an excerpt from my memoir, And Now, Back to Me: Stories from an Empty Nest. How this man responds when he finds out he needs to stay in the rehabilitation facility, when his heart had been set on coming home, is all you need to know about the man I am so lucky to call my father.

The man I'm lucky enough to call my father.
Source: Ernie Schenck

Ten minutes or so after it’s been decided that he needs to stay in the rehabilitation facility for another two weeks instead of going home as scheduled, my father leaves a long message on my phone. He makes a point of speaking slowly so that I can take notes. “Reets,” he says. “I need you to get some things from my house. My cell phone is in the little cubby in my car. It should be fully charged. But just in case, the charger is in your bedroom.” I love that he calls it my bedroom, even after all these years. “Also, I need stamps, address labels, and note cards, which you’ll find in the drawers of my desk. And don’t forget the thumbtacks.” He must mean paper clips. Yes, I’m sure he does. “I really appreciate you doing this for me. I don’t know what I’d do without you girls.”

When I arrive at the rehabilitation facility the next morning, his favorite Dunkin’ Donuts coffee in one hand, a bag filled with his requested supplies in the other, I watch him go about the business of setting up shop. Here, in the corner of his room, the nightstand has become his filing cabinet. His bedside table is now his desk. The rocker is his chair. And with that, he’s ready to go about conducting the daily routine of his life, keeping himself busy, making his days productive, no matter where he is or what circumstances he might find himself in.

Maybe his ability to make do with what he has, to make his home wherever he happens to find himself, was born out of necessity. Growing up the youngest of twenty-one children (not a typo!), he and his brothers and sisters ate dinner in shifts and slept three to a bed. If his childhood didn’t teach him enough about how to make the best of what was available, then joining the Navy at age eighteen was all the education he needed. He quickly learned to turn a mug of black Navy-issue coffee into a morning ritual; to express a genuine interest in other people’s lives, total strangers though they might be; and to appreciate beauty, even tucked away in a little sanctuary he made for himself on the deck of a ship while waiting for the sun to rise on an early-morning watch. That is how he made his way in the world from World War II to Korea to Vietnam, and all the places in between.

This way of his, this uncanny ability to accept what comes, to adapt and change course at a moment’s notice, lies at the core, in my opinion, of why he recently celebrated his ninety-second birthday. It’s not as though it’s been smooth sailing. It hasn’t. In the time since we lost Mom, his wife of sixty-three years, there have been heart ailments, a hip replacement, a broken wrist, a small stroke, a blood infection, and a stubborn gallstone. Yet always, there he was, rising to the occasion and finding a silver lining.

As we’ve traveled through these challenges together, he’s said to me many times, “I am where I am. I don’t know why. I’m not sure what’s coming at me next. But I’m grateful to be here, with all the love and care that surrounds me. Might as well make the best of it.”

Might as well make the best of it.

His words—which echo through my head along with the vision of my dad sitting at his “desk,” the bedside table in his rehabilitation room—are instructive as I go forward, arranging and rearranging the bits and pieces of my new way of empty-nest living. His inspiration reminds me that our attitude means more than any of our circumstances. Our mindset possesses the awesome power to change the course of our moments, our days, and, yes, our lives.

Lucky for me, I have his example to lead the way. I see him calling his relatives and friends to find out how they’re doing, going out to lunch whenever he gets the chance, sending notes of appreciation to all those who help make his days brighter. He's always showing genuine interest in the lives of those around him and finding ways to help however he can.

That acceptance of his, that grace of embracing whatever moment he finds himself in—perhaps shared mostly by example—that’s Dad’s best advice of all.

Taken to heart.

item.title: 'Cobwebbing' Can Help You Move On in Dating
item.description:
Mating

'Cobwebbing' Can Help You Move On in Dating

'Cobwebbing' can be scary, but you may scare off others if you don't do it.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • "Cobwebbing" means clearing away any "threads" that may be keeping you mentally or emotionally tied to an ex.
  • It entails getting rid of any physical and digital reminders of your ex and establishing clear boundaries.
  • Otherwise, your ex may end up living rent-free in your head and heart, leaving little room for anyone new.
  • If seems to hard to do, consider sweeping away everything all at once and getting someone to help you.
Are your head and heart filled with "cobwebs" from a previous relationship?
Source: New Africa/Shutterstock

Are your head and heart websites, so to speak—meaning, are they still filled with the remnants, or "cobwebs," of a previous relationship? Well, you might want to go "cobwebbing" then and remove all of them. "Cobwebbing," a term popularized by the dating app Bumble, means clearing away any "threads" that may be keeping you mentally or emotionally tied to an ex.

How Do You Do 'Cobwebbing'

This is not the same as spider-webbing, which I've described before for "A Funny Bone to Pick" as trapping someone in a bad, toxic relationship—a much creepier thing to do. No, cobwebbing is the opposite. It's about you getting away.

Cobwebbing entails getting rid of any physical reminders of your ex—like that Slanket that you used to cuddle together in, that alpaca figurine that was your birthday gift from your ex, or that lair that you used to share. Oh, and if your ex is somehow still hanging out with you in some way, your ex would qualify as a physical reminder of your ex.

Cobwebbing can be about simply discarding such objects or perhaps donating them to charity or someone else. Of course, some things—say, your ex or an apartment—may not be so easy to just throw down the trash chute or carry to Goodwill. In such cases, you may have to be the one who leaves and maintains as much physical distance as possible. This can include establishing very clear boundaries.

Oh, and don't forget about the digital reminders, too. That includes deleting your ex's digits—meaning that person's contact info—photos, messages, playlists, and other such things from your phone, watch, computer, and appliances. It can be a good idea to unfollow your ex on social media as well, because do you really need to see your ex post stuff like "Living my best life," "Humbled to share that...," or "Ugh, 20 people told me I looked hot today, so annoying?"

If you find it difficult to discard any of these things, that may be a clear sign that you are still holding on to your ex in some way. After all, nothing should be completely irreplaceable short of an original copy of Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa—which really should be in the Louvre, by the way—or the inventory logs for Area 51. The only other exception may be if you and your ex had kids together, which aren't so easy to put in the trash bin, of course.

Why Cobwebbing Can Be Important

Without such cobwebbing, the risk is that your ex will continue to haunt you—to live rent-free in your head and heart. And since both of those locations are like attics in that they don't have unlimited headroom and heartroom, such cobwebs may leave little space for anyone new. Still thinking about and having feelings for your ex—even if those feelings are resentment and hatred—could end up jeopardizing any future relationship.

Plus, chances are any potential quality dates—those who can sense who you are and what you are feeling—will also have some kind of Spidey sense for cobwebs in you. Such cobwebs can end up spooking them because no one of good quality will want to play second fiddle to an ex of yours for long. You could end up being like some kind of creepy attic where the only ones willing to enter are the ghouls and goblins.

Moreover, any remaining entanglements with your ex can keep you from moving on with your life in general. This can keep you caught cycling through denial, grief, regret, anger, resentment, and all those other emotions that accompany a breakup in the near term. As a result, you may never learn and heal properly from this previous relationship.

What If You Find Cobwebbing to Be Too Difficult

Now, getting rid of anything that's been a significant part of your life can initially seem scary. You may be tempted to hold on to keepsakes and the memories so that all the time you spent with your ex doesn't seem to be a waste. But tell yourself that it wasn't a waste, because the true keepsakes from previous relationships are the experience, lessons, and wisdom gained.

It may feel easier to gradually rid yourself of the cobwebs. That may work if you establish a clear end point and stay on schedule. The risk, otherwise, is procrastinating and stretching out the cobwebbing process to infinity and beyond.

Therefore, a better alternative may be choosing a single purge day to sweep away everything. While doing so, avoid examining or reading through anything too much—unless it contains something like key crypto account information or the map to help Odysseus return home to Ithaca. Otherwise, you may end up reminiscing and becoming too attached to the items.

If all of this is still too hard, then consider enlisting the aid of someone else, like a friend or a professional. Someone else may be more objective and, thus, more ruthless about tossing things. A friend can tell you stuff like, "Do you really need that banana slicer?"

Once you clear all the cobwebs, you may be pleasantly surprised at how clear your mind and heart feel as a result. Yes, it can be dangerous to stay on the web, so to speak, and remain haunted by an ex. Because it's only after your headroom and heartroom are truly clear of cobwebs that you can clear the way for someone new to move in—someone who may be a better fit for you.

item.title: Why Pregnancy Loss After Infertility Is More Than One Loss
item.description:
Pregnancy

Why Pregnancy Loss After Infertility Is More Than One Loss

When pregnancy finally starts, and then ends, the loss reaches beyond the pregnancy itself.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • A pregnancy loss after infertility often brings several losses at once, beyond the pregnancy itself.
  • Losing a long-waited pregnancy can take away the relief of finally knowing your body can get pregnant.
  • After a loss, a future pregnancy often comes with fear and bracing for bad news.
  • Letting go of the struggle to control the outcome can make it a littler easier to hope again.

When you get a positive test after years of trying to get pregnant, the joy is usually accompanied by some fear. After so long, your efforts finally worked—and now there’s something that could be taken away.

If that pregnancy, in turn, ends in a loss, there’s a distinct type of grief along with the disappointment and sadness, as well as a new kind of fear that compounds on top of the initial fear. This compounded fear comes from knowing now how painful it is, both physically and emotionally, to lose a pregnancy. This loss is layered because you are now grieving more than one loss.

The Loss of 'It Finally Worked'

If you've been struggling with infertility, getting pregnant is a relief. It finally worked, and you know your body can actually get pregnant. Losing that pregnancy can feel like having no say over what happens, with no guarantee that next time will be different.

Beyond proof your body can get pregnant, it can feel like the hard part is over. It may be the first time in a long time that you've let yourself plan.

If you've been in treatment, there’s often a moment of graduating from the fertility clinic to regular pregnancy care. After a loss, you go back to the clinic, the waiting room and the protocols, and it can feel like starting over from zero.

You may have followed every instruction this time, and it still ended, which can make the loss of control feel even greater.

Grieving More Than One Loss

When we think of grief, it is basically a response to loss. A loss can be tangible, emotional, or even imagined.

A pregnancy loss after infertility is complex because it involves losses at all these levels.

There's the loss of that reproductive story we imagined. Clients usually describe this timeline loss as a disruption in the order of things, at least the order many of us expect.

Then we have losses along the way: the loss of control, identity, belonging, hope, innocence, and the loss of planning.

Infertility and pregnancy loss also involve grieving a future. What makes this grief different is that it’s for something that never happened, something you wanted but never had.

When pregnancy finally happens, especially after fertility treatments, we get to see the light at the end of the tunnel. Unfortunately, 1 in 4 pregnancies end in a loss, which can make that moment very brief (Koert et al., 2023).

The Loss of Innocence in Pregnancy

Knowing it can be lost
Source: Envato/ Africaimages

A loss can also take away the joy of celebrating when a pregnancy happens again. In session, this is often described as losing the innocence of getting pregnant before knowing that it can be lost.

After one pregnancy loss, the brain learns that loss is very much possible. From then on, it holds both possibilities: a pregnancy that could continue and one that ends in loss. Since this loss can be significant and traumatic, it is now focused on the negative possibilities mostly to keep you safe from future suffering.

When the next pregnancy happens, there's no more of that carefree joy of planning the nursery, choosing baby names, and picking out cribs and newborn onesies. You are now experiencing the mature side of pregnancy after loss, and with the maturity comes the bracing for negative results. Couples who became pregnant again after a loss have described this as never being “pregnant in the same way again” (Koert et al., 2023). Clinicians call this anticipatory grief, when part of you starts grieving a loss before it happens.

Pregnancy after loss brings its own fears, especially after infertility and fertility treatments. Part of what makes it so hard is trying to hold on to hope that this time could end well. I wrote more about this in an earlier post, “The Trauma of Repeated Hope in Infertility.”

The Loss of Time and Treatment

Having gone through fertility treatments brings on even more losses, such as loss of a cycle, the money spent, and sometimes the last embryo.

There’s also the time. Each cycle takes weeks of appointments and waiting, and after a loss there’s often another wait before you can try again, while you’re aware of every month that passes.

In a recent study, women going through fertility treatment described the process as an “extended present,” where time moves back and forth between hope and uncertainty (Karaca Biçakçı et al., 2026). They also talked about their bodies becoming the focus of medical attention, and about the pressure they felt from the people around them. The researchers described infertility as a “biographical disruption,” something that changes how we see ourselves and where we fit in with others.

This study looked at women in treatment, and I see the same thing happen after a loss. When a pregnancy ends after fertility treatment, it can pull you right back into that extended present, just when the end finally seemed in sight. And this time, hope can feel harder to reach.

Letting Go of the Struggle for Control

Letting go of what you can’t hold
Source: Envato/MikeShots

Once you’ve lost a pregnancy after infertility, loss is no longer something that only happens to other people.

It’s understandable to want control over what happens next, especially after everything you’ve done to get here. A lot of the pain comes from the struggle itself, from trying to make sure it never happens again when so much of it was never in your hands.

In therapy, a big part of the work after a loss is letting go of that struggle to be in control. Of course, this is hard to do when so much of trying to conceive has already been about losing control.

When the struggle starts to ease, it often becomes a little easier to hope again, even with the fear still there.

item.title: The 3-Minute Rule for Having a Hard Talk
item.description:
Relationships

The 3-Minute Rule for Having a Hard Talk

Research suggests that how a tough conversation begins influences where it ends.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • How a couple begins a hard discussion can predict how the relationship looks years later.
  • Anger often flags moments when a partner’s goals interfere with our own.
  • Good timing, a gentle opening, and a neutral perspective may help hard talks go better.

While we might absolutely love our partner, sometimes knowing that we have to have a hard conversation makes us feel really negative. Maybe you lie awake working out exactly what you will say to your partner, and about a minute into the actual conversation, it has gone sideways. Maybe it was about the kids, or a furtive glance at a stranger. Maybe it was about money. Maybe it was about whose turn it is to empty the dishwasher, again. Experience has shown me that putting the talk off does not help much either.

The heart of these hard discussions is surprisingly direct. From an evolutionary perspective, conflict between partners is not a sign that love itself has failed. Buss (1989) proposed that conflict arises when one partner’s strategy interferes with the other’s goals, and that anger (among other feelings) is an emotional alarm signalling that interference. While the results of Buss’ study are mixed, it suggests a very simple insight, which is that the issues we find hardest to raise are often the ones where our interests and our partner’s do not really overlap.

In other words, the emotions you feel before a hard conversation provide valuable information and should not be ignored. They tell you that something matters to you. Is it your partner’s opinion? The outcome of the chat?

The challenge is delivering the information without setting off your partner’s alarms in return. The first three minutes are really going to matter. Carrère and Gottman (1999) filmed 124 newlywed couples arguing about something. Six years later, 17 of those couples had divorced, and they were couples who had started their arguments with more negativity and less warmth than those who stuck together did. Those critical three minutes at the start were enough to predict how the marriages turned out. What this means, at least to me, is that the opening for the hard discussion sets the tone. A conversation that begins with criticism or contempt leaves little room for anything positive to happen, whereas one that begins with some warmth, interest, or humor gives both people a chance to be positive. There is room for something other than negativity.

When having a hard discussion, most of us know that we should try to be present and open for our partner. Most of us also know that we have to be wary of the classic demand-withdraw pattern, where one partner pushes for change, often with criticism or blame, while the other avoids the topic, becomes defensive, and pulls away. A meta-analysis of 74 studies with more than 14,000 participants linked the pattern to lower relationship satisfaction, less intimacy, and poorer communication (Schrodt et al., 2014). What might be missed, though, is what this pattern is saying, which is that the partner who wants more change on the topic under discussion is more likely to demand, while the partner who wants less change may be more likely to withdraw (Holley et al., 2010).

We also know that emotions can be modified by food, and prepping for a hard conversation is particularly susceptible to hunger. Bushman and colleagues (2014) tracked blood sugar in married couples over three weeks. In one of my all-time favourite study designs, each evening, participants stuck pins into a voodoo doll representing their spouse, depending on how angry they felt. (Does science get any better?) More pins were correlated with lower evening glucose levels. Lange and Kurzban (2014) have questioned whether this is really about self-control, but in any case, the practical lesson seems low risk, which is do not open a difficult topic when either of you is hungry, or worse, “hangry.”

One final consideration that might be worth a thought is to imagine how an objective observer would view your discussion. Over two years, Finkel and colleagues (2013) followed 120 married couples. In year two, half of the couples spent just seven minutes, three times over the year, writing about their most recent disagreement from the perspective of a neutral third party who wants the best for everyone involved. While average marital quality declined for both groups in the first year, the decline stopped for those who did the writing, but not for the other couples.

Now, for some tips. Let’s start with remembering that, above all else, the first three minutes matter when starting a hard conversation.

  1. Choose your timing. Raise the topic after a meal rather than when either of you is hungry. Over a dessert and coffee is a perfect time to not rush and have a good chat.
  2. Open gently and with kindness. Begin with something warm or appreciative before going directly to the issue, given that early positive emotion distinguished the couples who stayed together.
  3. Think about what matters to you. Treat your anger or other emotions as a signal of what you need, and state that need rather than listing your partner’s faults, after you have started the conversation.
  4. Try to consider the situation from the angle of an objective observer. Before you begin, or after a talk if it goes badly, take a few minutes to picture the disagreement the way a fair-minded friend who wants the best for you both would. Reflect on that and allow that to help influence future discussion.

While I would personally love to think otherwise, difficult conversations will never be easy, and perhaps they should not be, given that they tend to arise where two people’s interests are not aligned. When they do happen, a warm and positive first few minutes, a full stomach, and a little distance from the fight may help the person you love actually hear you.

item.title: When 'Love at First Sight' Gets in the Way of Love
item.description:
Relationships

When 'Love at First Sight' Gets in the Way of Love

Why lasting love takes more than a spark.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Family experiences can shape commitment fears without determining a relationship’s future.
  • Immediate attraction cannot establish how partners will handle differences over time.
  • Hiding important needs to avoid conflict can limit opportunities for understanding and closeness.

My husband and I have been married almost 25 years. He maintains that it was love at first sight; I maintain that he is mistaken. Regardless of who is correct, as a family scientist, I recognize that beliefs like love at first sight can contribute to myths about romantic love that can negatively impact relationships. Hallmark movies, like other romance movies, tend to be based on these myths, including the belief in soulmates or that love can conquer all. In real life, the more one believes in these myths, the less likely they are to be in satisfying relationships. Some may even end their relationships before they experience conflict out of the belief that, if they were truly meant to be, there should be no conflict.

In Hallmark’s Forgotten Holiday, we see a couple who subscribes to myths about romantic love and watch as they decide whether they want to move past those myths to find authentic love or go their separate ways.

"Forgotten Holiday"
Source: Hallmark Media

Love at Second Sight?

Hallmark’s Forgotten Holiday introduces us to Rob Ashford and Kathryn Liu. For Rob, it’s love at first sight. Rob proposes at the start of the holiday season since that is his favorite time of year. Kathryn’s fear of failed relationships, fueled by her parents’ divorce as well as her own, has her bolting from the proposal without giving Rob an answer. Confused and heartbroken, he drives to his sister’s house but gets into an accident that leaves him with amnesia. His memories quickly return except for his memories of Kathryn. The doctor prescribes the unconventional therapy that Rob and Kathryn re-date. As his memories return, he eventually remembers the way their relationship ended.

Hallmark has used amnesia to spark relationship development, improvement, or evaluation in previous movies. In this case, it allows Kathryn to understand how her fear of commitment impacted their relationship and allows Rob to identify what he truly wants out of a romantic partner. Amnesia provides an opportunity for both to learn more about themselves and each other, but they each need to make the choice to do so.

Authenticity in Relationships

Rob’s and Kathryn’s efforts to recreate their previous relationship fall flat. He repeatedly reminds her that he is not “old Rob”; perhaps he is also reminding himself. I found myself cringing at the awkwardness of their re-dating attempts. Things go so poorly that they question how they dated for an entire year. Viewers may be left wondering the same, feeling like Rob and Kathryn can’t seem to be themselves around one another.

We can face a similar challenge in off-screen relationships. Imagine agreeing to every holiday plan while quietly wanting something different, pretending to share an interest because disagreement feels risky, or withholding worries about the future to preserve a happy evening. The intention is understandable, especially if we also feel that we need to choose our battles and protect our connections. But when we're hiding preferences, conforming to partners’ opinions, and withholding needs, we give our partner fewer opportunities to understand us, respond to us, or discover where we differ.

In one study, researchers found that concealing personal information from a partner was associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment. This daily diary study also linked concealment with poorer relationship well-being. Authenticity doesn’t mean sharing every thought or giving up privacy, but when we consistently hide important parts of ourselves, we limit the opportunity to discover whether our partner can know and accept us.

Love Built Through Everyday Choices

One of my favorite scenes comes towards the end of the movie. Kathryn’s father suggests that negative relationship outcomes emerge from choices rather than a doomed-to-be-alone fate. His observation leaves room for agency: We cannot control everything that happens in a relationship, but we can consider how our choices shape the connections we build.

Those choices may seem ordinary but can have a strong impact on the relationship. We can speak honestly about uncertainty instead of pretending to feel sure. We can let a partner express a different preference without treating it as evidence that they aren’t a soulmate. We can ask questions rather than assume what a disagreement means, address hurt instead of hiding it, and examine which expectations we carry from our family experiences. These choices won’t guarantee that a relationship will last, but they can help us understand ourselves and each other more clearly. This can help us build an authentic relationship.

"Forgotten Holiday"
Source: Hallmark Media

In Forgotten Holiday, amnesia creates the interruption that allows Kathryn and Rob to reconsider their relationship. It is a dramatic storytelling device, but we don’t need to wait until a dramatic interruption happens to reflect on our relationships.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark: If it’s true love, the spark will bring you back together—even if it takes amnesia and a second first date.

Psychology: That initial spark can draw us to someone, but it cannot build or sustain a relationship. Romantic partners need to commit to getting to know each other, make room for differences, and be honest even when the conversation feels uncomfortable.

The verdict: Forgotten Holiday earns points for letting its couple question the romance they once accepted. Their second chance matters because it offers an opportunity to know each other more honestly. Fortunately, the rest of us can begin without a case of amnesia.
